title: Book II: Old And Young — Chapter XX
paragraphs:
“A child forsaken, waking suddenly,
Whose gaze afeard on all things round doth rove,
And seeth only that it cannot see
The meeting eyes of love.”
Two hours later Dorothea sat in an inner room, a boudoir, of an elegant apartment in the Via Sistina.

I am sorry to say she was sobbing bitterly. She surrendered to the relief of an overburdened heart as a woman usually restrained by personal pride and consideration for others will sometimes allow herself to do when she knows she is alone. Mr. Casaubon was certain to remain at the Vatican for some time.

Yet Dorothea had no clear grievance she could explain even to herself. Amid her tangled thoughts and feelings, the idea struggling towards clarity was an accusation against herself: her desolation must arise from her own spiritual poverty. She had married the man she chose. Unlike most girls, she had chiefly looked forward to marriage as the beginning of new duties. From the outset she had considered Mr. Casaubon’s mind so far above her own that studies she could not fully share must often occupy him. Besides, after the brief, narrow experience of her girlhood, she was seeing Rome, the city of visible history, where a whole hemisphere’s past seems to move in a funeral procession, bearing strange ancestral images and trophies gathered from distant lands.

But those tremendous fragments only deepened the dreamlike strangeness of her married life. Dorothea had spent five weeks in Rome. On the gentle mornings when autumn and winter seemed to walk hand in hand like a happy elderly couple, one of whom would soon survive in colder loneliness, she had driven out, at first with Mr. Casaubon and more recently chiefly with Tantripp and their experienced traveling attendant. She had been guided through the finest galleries, taken to the principal viewpoints, shown the grandest ruins and most glorious churches. In the end she most often chose to drive onto the Campagna, where she could feel alone with earth and sky, away from the oppressive masquerade of centuries in which her own life too seemed to become a pageant in puzzling costumes.

For those who have seen Rome through knowledge that gives life and a growing soul to every historical form, tracing the hidden transitions that join its contrasts, the city may remain the world’s spiritual center and interpreter. But let them imagine one further historical contrast. The huge, broken revelations of that imperial and papal city were thrust suddenly upon the understanding of a girl raised in English and Swiss Puritanism, fed on scant Protestant histories and art chiefly of the kind used to decorate hand screens. Her passionate nature turned every scrap of knowledge into a principle and shaped her actions in its mold; her quick feelings made even the most abstract things sources of pleasure or pain. Newly married, she had passed from an enthusiastic welcome for untried duty into a turbulent preoccupation with her own fate. Unintelligible Rome might rest lightly on bright young nymphs who used it as the backdrop for the glittering picnic of English society abroad. Dorothea had no such protection from profound impressions. Ruins and basilicas, palaces and colossal statues stood amid a shabby present, where living, warm-blooded humanity seemed sunk in the degradation of superstition emptied of reverence. A dimmer but still eager life of titanic figures stared and struggled on walls and ceilings. Long avenues of white statues looked out with marble eyes that seemed to hold the monotonous light of an alien world. This vast wreckage of ambitious ideals, sensual and spiritual, mingled confusedly with signs of living forgetfulness and decay. At first it jarred her like an electric shock; then it pressed upon her with the ache of too many tangled ideas blocking the flow of feeling. Figures pale and glowing took possession of her young senses and settled into memory even when she was not thinking of them, forming strange associations that stayed with her for years. Our moods often bring images that follow one another like projected pictures seen while dozing. All her life, in certain states of dull loneliness, Dorothea would continue to see the immense interior of St. Peter’s, its enormous bronze canopy, the urgent purpose in the poses and robes of the prophets and evangelists in the mosaics overhead, and the red hangings being put up for Christmas, spreading everywhere like a disorder of the eye.

Dorothea’s inward bewilderment was hardly exceptional. Many souls, still naked in youth, are tumbled into a world of inconsistencies and left to find their footing while their elders attend to business. Nor do I imagine anyone will consider it tragic to discover Mrs. Casaubon crying six weeks after her wedding. Some discouragement, some sinking of the heart when an actual future replaces the imagined one, is common enough. We do not expect people to be deeply moved by ordinary things. The tragedy contained in their very frequency has not yet entered humanity’s coarse feelings; perhaps our bodies could scarcely bear much of it. If we could see and feel ordinary human life acutely, it would be like hearing grass grow and a squirrel’s heart beat. We would die of the roar on the other side of silence. As things are, even the most sensitive of us move about comfortably padded with stupidity.

Still, Dorothea was crying. Asked why, she could only have answered in the general terms I have already used. To press her for particulars would have been like asking for a history of lights and shadows. The real future replacing her imagined one was being formed from endless tiny details. Through them, her understanding of Mr. Casaubon and of herself as his wife was changing as imperceptibly as a watch hand moves, away from her unmarried dream. It was too soon for her fully to recognize, or at least admit, the change; still less could she have redirected the devotion so essential to her inner life that she was almost certain to recover it sooner or later. Lasting rebellion, the disorder of a life without some loving and reverent purpose, was impossible for her. But she was passing through an interval in which her nature’s very strength intensified its confusion. The first months of marriage often bring such critical turbulence, whether in a shrimp pool or deeper waters, before settling into cheerful peace.

Yet was Mr. Casaubon not as learned as before? Had his manner of speaking changed, or his principles become less admirable? Oh, the fickleness of women! Had his command of dates failed, or his ability to state both a theory and the names of its supporters, or his readiness to outline any subject on request? And where better than Rome to display those accomplishments? Besides, had Dorothea’s enthusiasm not centered on easing the burden, perhaps the sadness, that great tasks impose upon the person charged with completing them? That such a burden weighed on Mr. Casaubon was merely clearer than before.

These questions are crushing. But whatever else stayed the same, the light had changed, and you cannot find the pearly dawn at noon. One fact remains unavoidable: a fellow human being known only through brief appearances and departures during a few imaginative weeks called courtship may, in the continuous companionship of marriage, prove better or worse than expected, but will certainly not seem exactly the same. The speed of that change would astonish us if we had no similar changes for comparison. Sharing rooms with a brilliant dinner companion, or seeing a favorite politician enter government, can transform our judgment just as quickly. There too we begin by knowing little and believing much, and sometimes end with the quantities reversed.

Those comparisons could mislead, however. No one was less capable of dazzling pretense than Mr. Casaubon. He was as genuine as any cud-chewing animal and had done nothing actively to create illusions about himself. Why, then, in the weeks since her marriage, had Dorothea felt, without clearly observing it, that the wide views and fresh air she had expected in her husband’s mind were replaced by waiting rooms and winding corridors leading nowhere? The feeling oppressed her almost to suffocation. I suppose that during courtship everything appears provisional and preliminary. The smallest sample of virtue or accomplishment guarantees delightful reserves that the broad leisure of marriage will reveal. Once across marriage’s threshold, however, expectation fixes on the present. Having embarked on the marital voyage, one cannot help noticing that the vessel makes no progress and the sea is nowhere in sight; that one is, in fact, exploring an enclosed basin.

Before their marriage, Mr. Casaubon had often lingered over explanations or disputed details whose relevance Dorothea could not see. She attributed the imperfect connection to the interruptions in their time together. Faith in their future sustained her, and she listened with passionate patience as he recited possible objections to his entirely new theory of the Philistine god Dagon and other fish deities. Later, she thought, she would see this subject, so close to his heart, from the same high ground that had surely made it important to him. Likewise, when he treated thoughts that stirred her deeply as obvious matters to be dismissed, she could explain his manner by the haste and distraction she too felt during their engagement. But now, in Rome, with her deepest feelings in tumult and new experiences making life itself a new problem, she became increasingly and fearfully aware that her mind kept slipping into inward bursts of anger and aversion, or into lonely exhaustion. She had no way of knowing how the judicious Hooker or any other hero of learning might have behaved at Mr. Casaubon’s age, so he gained nothing by comparison. Her husband’s comments on the strangely powerful objects around them had begun to send a kind of shiver through her mind. He might earnestly intend to perform his part creditably, but merely to perform it. What was fresh to her had long been worn out for him. Whatever capacity for thought and feeling the general life of humanity had once awakened in him had long ago dried into a preserved specimen, a lifeless embalming of knowledge.

When he said, “Does this interest you, Dorothea? Shall we remain a little longer? I am willing to stay if you wish,” staying and leaving seemed equally dreary. Or he might ask, “Would you care to visit the Farnesina, Dorothea? It contains celebrated frescoes designed or painted by Raphael, which most people consider worth seeing.”
“But do YOU care about them?” Dorothea always asked.

“They are highly regarded, I believe. Some depict the story of Cupid and Psyche, probably a romantic invention of a literary age rather than a genuine product of mythology. But if these wall paintings appeal to you, we can easily drive there. You will then, I think, have seen Raphael’s principal works, any of which it would be unfortunate to miss on a visit to Rome. He is considered the painter who most perfectly combines grace of form with sublimity of expression. At least, I understand that to be the experts’ opinion.”

Such answers, delivered in a measured official tone like a clergyman reading exactly as directed, did nothing to vindicate the Eternal City’s glories. Nor did they give her hope that greater knowledge would illuminate the world with joy. Few encounters depress a passionate young person more than contact with a mind in which years of accumulated knowledge seem to have produced a blank absence of interest or sympathy.

On other subjects, certainly, Mr. Casaubon showed the persistence and eagerness usually taken as signs of enthusiasm. Dorothea longed to follow the natural direction of his thoughts rather than feel she was dragging him away from them. Yet she was gradually losing her former joyful confidence that following him would lead to any broad opening. Poor Mr. Casaubon himself was lost among small cupboards and twisting stairways. In his agitated obscurity about the Cabeiri, or his exposure of other mythologists’ careless comparisons, he easily lost sight of whatever purpose had first driven his labors. With a candle fixed before him, he forgot the lack of windows. Writing bitter manuscript comments on other men’s theories of sun gods, he had ceased to care about sunlight.

These traits, as fixed and unchangeable in Mr. Casaubon as bone, might have escaped Dorothea’s notice longer if he had encouraged her to pour out her feelings as a girl and a woman. He might have held her hands in his and listened with tender, understanding pleasure to the little histories making up her experience, then offered the same intimacy in return, so that each person’s past became part of their shared knowledge and affection. Or she might have nourished her love with those childlike caresses natural to every affectionate woman who began by kissing the hard, bald head of her doll, creating a happy soul inside the wood from the abundance of her own love. That was Dorothea’s inclination. For all her longing to understand distant things and spread goodness widely, she had enough passion for what was near to kiss Mr. Casaubon’s sleeve or caress the fastening of his shoe. She only needed some sign of acceptance beyond his impeccably proper declaration that she possessed a most affectionate and truly feminine nature, while politely drawing up a chair to indicate that he found these displays somewhat crude and startling. Once he had carefully dressed in his clerical clothes each morning, he was prepared only for those civilities suited to the period’s neatly adjusted stiff cravat and a mind burdened with unpublished material.

By a sad contradiction, Dorothea’s ideas and resolutions seemed like melting ice, floating and vanishing in the warm flood of which they had merely been another form. She was ashamed to find herself helpless before feeling, as though it were the only means by which she could know anything. Her strength scattered itself in bursts of agitation, struggle, and despair, then in visions of more complete self-denial that would turn every hardship into duty. Poor Dorothea! She was certainly troublesome, chiefly to herself. But that morning, for the first time, she had troubled Mr. Casaubon.

Over coffee she had begun by resolving to shake off what she privately called selfishness. She turned towards her husband with cheerful attention when he said, “My dear Dorothea, we must now consider everything that remains to be done before our departure. I would gladly have returned sooner, so that we might spend Christmas at Lowick, but my inquiries here have lasted longer than expected. I trust, however, that your time has not passed unpleasantly. Among Europe’s sights, Rome has always been considered one of the most impressive and, in some respects, instructive. I well remember regarding my first visit as a landmark in my life. It was after Napoleon’s fall, which reopened the Continent to travelers. Indeed, I believe Rome is one of several cities to which that extreme exaggeration has been applied: ‘See Rome and die.’ In your case, though, I would amend it: See Rome as a bride, and live afterwards as a happy wife.”

Mr. Casaubon delivered this little speech with the most conscientious intentions, blinking slightly, moving his head up and down, and finishing with a smile. He had not found marriage a state of rapture. But he intended to be nothing less than a husband beyond reproach, making a charming young woman as happy as she deserved.
“I hope you’re completely satisfied with our stay—with what you’ve accomplished in your studies, I mean,” said Dorothea, trying to keep her thoughts on what mattered most to him.

“Yes,” Mr. Casaubon replied in that particular tone that makes the word half a refusal. “I have been drawn farther than I anticipated. Various subjects requiring notes have presented themselves, which I could not pass over although I have no immediate use for them. Even with my secretary’s assistance, the task has been rather laborious. Happily, your company has prevented the excessive continuation of thought beyond working hours that has so often ensnared my solitary life.”

“I’m very glad my presence has made any difference,” said Dorothea. She vividly remembered evenings when she had supposed his mind had sunk too deeply during the day to reach the surface again. I fear her answer held a little irritation. “When we return to Lowick, I hope I can be more useful and share more of what interests you.”
“Certainly, my dear,” said Mr. Casaubon with a slight bow. “The notes I have made here will require sorting. If you wish, you may make extracts under my direction.”

“And all your other notes,” Dorothea said. Her heart had already burned over this subject, and now her tongue could not remain silent. “All those rows of volumes—won’t you do what you used to talk about? Won’t you decide which parts to use and begin the book that will make your immense knowledge useful to the world? I’ll take your dictation, or copy and extract whatever you ask. I can be useful in no other way.” With that inexplicable behavior so mysteriously attributed to women, Dorothea ended in a little sob, her eyes full of tears.

The intensity of her feeling alone would have disturbed Mr. Casaubon considerably. But there were further reasons why these words were among the most wounding and irritating she could have chosen. She was as unaware of his inward troubles as he was of hers. She had not yet learned the hidden conflicts in him that call for our pity. She had not listened patiently to his heartbeat, only felt her own beating violently. To Mr. Casaubon’s ears her voice loudly repeated those muffled suggestions of his own awareness that he could otherwise explain away as imagination, as the illusion of excessive sensitivity. When such suggestions are unmistakably repeated from outside, we always resist them as cruel and unjust. Even complete agreement with our humiliating confessions can anger us. How much worse to hear a close observer speak, in hard, clear syllables, the confused murmurs we try to dismiss as unhealthy and fight against as though they were the onset of numbness! And this cruel outside accuser was his wife—his young bride. Instead of regarding his abundant pen marks and masses of paper with the uncritical awe of a refined canary, she seemed to stand before him as a spy, watching everything with a malicious gift for inference. On this particular point Mr. Casaubon was as sensitive as Dorothea, and just as quick to imagine more than the facts. Earlier he had approvingly noticed her capacity to worship the proper object. Now he suddenly feared that presumption might replace it, that worship might turn into the most irritating criticism of all: the kind that vaguely sees many splendid goals without the least understanding of what reaching them costs.
For the first time since Dorothea had known him, anger flushed Mr. Casaubon’s face.

“My love,” he said, keeping his irritation within the reins of propriety, “you may trust me to know the appropriate times and stages of a work that cannot be measured by the easy guesses of ignorant spectators. I could readily have created a passing impression with a mirage of unsupported opinion. But the painstaking investigator must always endure the impatient contempt of talkers who attempt only the smallest achievements, being equipped for nothing greater. It would be well if such people learned to distinguish between judgments whose subject lies entirely beyond their understanding and those whose elements can be grasped in a narrow, superficial survey.”

He spoke with an energy and fluency unusual for him. The speech was not entirely improvised. It had formed in inward conversation and now burst out like round seeds from a fruit split by sudden heat. Dorothea was more than his wife: she embodied the shallow world surrounding the appreciated or discouraged author.
Now Dorothea was angry too. Had she not suppressed everything in herself except the desire to share her husband’s main interests?

“My judgment WAS superficial, as any judgment I can form must be,” she replied with an immediate resentment that needed no rehearsal. “You showed me the rows of notebooks. You’ve often spoken about them and said they needed arranging. But I’ve never heard you speak of writing anything for publication. Those were simple facts, and my judgment went no further. I only asked you to let me be of some use.”

Dorothea rose from the table. Mr. Casaubon did not answer, but picked up a letter beside him as though to reread it. Both were shocked by their position: each had shown anger towards the other. At home, settled into ordinary life among their neighbors at Lowick, the clash would have been less awkward. On a honeymoon, whose express purpose is to isolate two people because they are everything to each other, disagreement is at the least bewildering and discrediting. To travel far across the globe and place yourselves in emotional solitude, only to have small explosions, struggle for conversation, and pass a glass of water without meeting eyes, can scarcely seem a satisfactory result even to the toughest minds. To Dorothea’s inexperienced sensitivity it felt like a catastrophe altering every prospect. For Mr. Casaubon it was a new kind of pain. He had never been on a honeymoon or entered this close union, which involved more subjection than he had imagined. The charming young bride not only required much consideration, which he had diligently provided; she also proved capable of distressing him cruelly at the very point where he most needed comfort. Instead of gaining a soft barrier against the cold, shadowy, unapproving audience of his life, had he merely given that audience a more solid presence?

Neither felt able to speak again just then. Canceling their planned outing would have displayed a continuing anger from which Dorothea’s conscience recoiled, especially as she was already beginning to feel guilty. However justified her indignation, her ideal was to offer tenderness rather than demand justice. So when the carriage arrived, she drove with Mr. Casaubon to the Vatican and walked beside him through the stone avenue of inscriptions. At the Library entrance they parted, and she continued through the Museum from sheer indifference to her surroundings. She lacked the energy to turn and say she wanted to drive somewhere. Naumann had first seen her as Mr. Casaubon left her, and had entered the long sculpture gallery at the same time. There he had to wait for Ladislaw, with whom he was to settle a bet of champagne over a puzzling figure of medieval appearance. They examined it and walked on, finishing their dispute, then separated. Ladislaw lingered behind while Naumann went into the Hall of Statues. There he saw Dorothea again, lost in the brooding abstraction that made her pose remarkable. She no more saw the sunlight on the floor than she saw the statues. Inwardly she was seeing the light of future years in her own home and across the English fields, elms, and hedge-lined roads. She felt less certain than before how those years could be filled with joyful devotion. But her mind contained a current into which all thought and feeling sooner or later flowed: the whole of her awareness reaching towards the fullest truth and the good least confined to self. Clearly there was something better than anger and despair.
